title: Disagreeing without drawing blood
description: You can argue with an idea and still leave the person holding it completely intact.

body.heading: Aim at the idea, not the person
paragraphs: “That plan will not work because the shop closes at five” is an argument. “You never think things through” is a wound. The first can be answered; the second can only be defended against.
A useful habit is to ban the words “always” and “never” from disagreements. They are almost never true, and they invite the other person to argue about the exaggeration instead of the point.

body.heading: Steelman before you answer
paragraphs: Before you reply, try stating the other person’s view so fairly that they say, “Yes, that’s what I mean.” It feels slow, but it is the fastest way to find out what you actually disagree about — which is often smaller than it first seemed.
Sometimes you will discover you agree about the facts and only differ about what matters most. That is a much kinder argument to have.

body.heading: Leave a way back
paragraphs: End disagreements with a door open: “Let’s think about it overnight,” or “I might be wrong about the middle part.” People change their minds in private far more easily than in public, under pressure.
Winning an argument and keeping the relationship are both possible, but rarely by the same sentence. Choose which one each sentence is for.

takeaway: Argue with the idea, state the other side fairly, and always leave a way back.
